title: Complex Agony
story:
In 2011 I was in 11th grade at Birla School in Pilani. The school had no formal art classes, but with the encouragement of my art teacher, Prakash Khandey, I took the leap onto stretched canvas. Once the others saw me start, nine more students joined in and painted their own canvases in the school art room. I worked on this one during school hours and quiet evenings for nearly a whole year, eight to twelve months on a single canvas.

At the centre stands a girl who has been stabbed, with blood staining her t-shirt. Yet she refuses to be a victim: she presses both hands tightly over her heart. To match the weight of that image, I didn't use normal brushwork. I rubbed dense linseed oil paint into the raw canvas with my hands and a cloth, for hours at a time, until the agony felt worked into the fabric itself. The darkness around her isn't flat black either. I mixed it from layered glazes of vermilion, burnt umber and Prussian blue, so it feels alive.

Complex Agony isn't about defeat; it's about fiercely protecting yourself. The world can wound the outside, the shirt and the body, but her hands guard the core: the heart and the soul. It sold at the 21-day Serendipity exhibition in Jaipur, and the thrill of that first sale quickly turned into grief and emptiness. It taught me early that my canvases aren't products. They are living pieces of who I am.

title: Splendid Soul
story:
By 2012 I was in 12th grade. After the closed-in feeling of Complex Agony, I wanted to go big: this canvas is 120 × 150 cm, the largest of my early works. I painted it over six to seven months, during school hours and evenings in the Birla School art room, and it was the first time I invested in large professional tubes of single colours, especially bright reds.

A girl stands alone at the centre, beneath a big tree that fills the background and the top of the canvas. She holds open the fold of her frock to catch the autumn leaves falling from above. I wanted the leaves to feel real, so I gathered fallen leaves from the ground, coated them in heavy vermilion and crimson oil glazes, and pressed them straight onto the canvas.

If Complex Agony was about closing and protecting the heart against a wound, Splendid Soul is about opening it. The open frock gathers grace in the middle of all the struggle inside. It holds that short, splendid time of youth just before you become an adult, and shows that beauty and strength can live right inside the chaos.

title: The Urban Hermit
story:
The Urban Hermit was my own Independence Day. For the first time, I moved out of the shared Birla School art room and painted at home in Pilani, in a room that was all mine. With no school bells and no teachers or classmates watching, my pace changed completely: instead of spending a year on a canvas, I finished this one in a single week of all-night sessions.

Across the wide 45 × 77 cm canvas, a deep, many-layered black fills the centre and the right side. Pushed all the way to the far-left edge sits a girl deep in thought, pressing her hands against her head and resting her chin in her palms to block out the noise. Here I learned that black on canvas is never flat; it's a balance of hidden tones underneath that makes the darkness feel alive.

This is where the hermit in my work began. Placing her at the very edge of that empty space was my way of showing what isolation feels like today: choosing midnight silence to protect your peace and find your own voice before stepping out into the loud marketplace of the world.

title: Nothing on you
story:
If my first painting took a year and the third took a week of all-nighters, Nothing on you was a lightning strike. I locked myself in my home studio in Pilani and painted straight through one day and one night, 24 hours without a break, and finished the whole canvas in a single sitting.

I painted it wet-on-wet and fast. The figure has striking lime-blonde, greenish parted hair and glowing, flushed crimson and blush-pink highlights against cool, muted indigo and slate shadows. Because it all came out in one 24-hour flow, the brushwork still has that electric, unhesitating energy.

That session taught me one of the hardest lessons in painting: knowing when to stop. Good work doesn't always need months of overthinking; sometimes you have to outrun your self-doubt and trust your instinct. The title is about the subject's untouchable presence, and about a canvas with nothing overworked or fake added to it.

title: Strings Teem Senses
story:
After four intense figurative paintings, Strings Teem Senses was my first real leap into pure abstraction. I played guitar in my school band, and I didn't just listen to music; I felt the vibration and tension of the strings under my fingertips. I wanted to put that feeling on canvas, so I split one picture across three separate 45 × 45 cm canvases.

The idea comes from the guitar and its standard tuning (EADGBe), but I chose the classic shape of a violin to carry it. When the three panels hang side by side, the instrument appears: the violin's bow sweeps out of the left panel, cuts through the heart of the centre canvas and comes to rest on the right.

This is where the musician and the painter in me met. By breaking the instrument across three canvases, I let your eye put the melody back together across the silent gaps between them, and I realised I no longer needed a face to show deep human emotion.

title: Gaol of Greed
story:
Gaol of Greed ("Jail of Greed") is my second purely abstract painting. I made it at home in Pilani just after the national group exhibition at Jawahar Kala Kendra in Jaipur, before my 12th board exams kept me busy with studies. After breaking down musical harmony in Strings Teem Senses, I turned abstraction towards mapping raw emotional and social pressure.

The horizontal 60 × 83 cm canvas is split between two opposing forces. In the top right, a stormy, swirling vortex of crimson and burgundy stands for the "Circle of Life" and the intoxicating loop of ambition. Balancing it in the bottom left is an airy, smoky golden-yellow field with rising vertical stalks and grounded, burdened human figures carrying the heavy pull of material desire.

My first four paintings looked inward, at the self. Gaol of Greed was my first look at the system outside, a decade before the Richie series. It maps the "mixture of pure emotions" that comes when ambition hardens into a prison, a "gaol", of material things.

title: Trying and Being
story:
After my 12th board exams I stepped away from painting for a while, and a lot happened in that time. When I came back to the canvas in 2014, I changed my whole style to deal with everything I was carrying. Trying and Being is the first painting in that new style, and the next few works followed it.

On a square 60 × 60 cm canvas, an expressive face gazes up and to the right, in muted teal and cyan, warm ochre, deep crimson and smoky slate-black textures. Vertical drips run down the surface and keep the raw physical energy of that session.

The title holds the friction I felt then, between trying to become something and simply being who you are. It's also about showing up to the canvas and doing the work, even when you're questioning the process.

title: Now you see me, now you don't
story:
I painted this in Pilani in 2014, during a very inward-looking time for me. It's about being seen and hiding: the social masks we choose to wear to get through what people expect of us.

It's a haunting, cool-toned vertical portrait (60 × 45 cm) in washed slate blue, charcoal black and stark white highlights. Half of the face dissolves into textured marks, while a vivid crimson wash slashes across one eye and drips down the canvas.

It asks how vulnerable it is to let yourself be seen: how much of what's really going on inside we show the world before we retreat behind our filters.

title: The Stripped Tint
story:
In my early archive I gave this one the subtitle "Ethics in Action". With The Stripped Tint I turned the painting inward, towards conscience, moral weight and humility.

Against a muted white background, a distressed figure bows forward, clutching their head in both hands. Heavy, raw brushstrokes of forest green, deep crimson, ochre and peach carve the pose out of the empty space.

By stripping away decorative colour, the "tint", I wanted to ask what's left of a person's character and integrity once the applause, the ego and all the distractions are taken away.

title: The One Who Knew
story:
I painted The One Who Knew in 2014. It's about the silent weight of memory: the unspoken truths and lessons we carry with us through time.

It's a close-up, expressive face glancing sideways, lit up by fiery crimson and orange hair, with earthy umber shadows, contrasting teal-blue lips and paint dripping down like tears.

For me it's an anchor for memory, a reminder that our own past holds quiet realisations we can't run away from, and that wisdom is often found in quietly watching.

title: Sneak Peak
story:
Sneak Peak was my very first exploration of querencia: the search for an inner sanctuary, a place where you feel completely safe and at home.

It's an over-the-shoulder portrait framed by a bold, bubblegum-pink silhouette of hair, with warm ochre and emerald highlights on the face, deep crimson undertones and layers of drips cascading over charcoal black.

True to its name, it gives a quick glimpse over the shoulder into my private inner world, a first preview of the peace I would fully find seven years later in Sydney, with Querencia.

title: The Doomed One
story:
The Doomed One closes my first era. Before this canvas I hadn't painted for a while, and things were hard with people close to me. I was angry and anxious, so I sat down and painted to sort myself out.

A solitary figure sits hunched forward in profile, carved out of dripping washes of olive drab, muted chartreuse yellow, dark moss green and slate grey. The features are blurred and heavy with thick paint, like a soul struggling against the weight of its own thoughts.

When I shared it, I paired it with these words: "What is presence and what is its relationship to painting? So we learn our skills, locate what is real for us, show up, and paint." She looks doomed, but painting her is what saved me.

title: Blue Winds
story:
I painted Blue Winds in New Delhi in 2015. It's no longer with me, but I still remember making it, and this photograph is how the painting lives on.

A crouched figure, head bowed onto her knees, half dissolves into washes of moss, olive and yellow-green. Dark hair falls forward, and soft vertical strokes sweep across the background like wind moving through leaves.

title: Strangers in the night
story:
When I started this canvas in Delhi in 2016, I felt it would be my best painting yet. It began as a completely different painting and changed as I worked: I painted one face, then painted a new face over it. That first face is still hidden beneath the one you see.

It's a fierce, direct close-up glowing with fiery orange and crimson, set against cobalt-teal lips, dark charcoal shadows and paint dripping down like tears.

Strangers in the night is about the electric, anonymous moments of crowded city nights: the brief, unspoken heat between strangers passing in the dark.

title: Burnt Wine
story:
Burnt Wine is my first mixed media painting, and the name is literal. I was painting in Delhi with a glass of wine in my hand when the power went out, so I lit the room with candles and started dripping wax onto the canvas. Then I held a flame close, saw the surface start to blacken, and decided to try burning the painting on purpose. When I realised it was really burning, I put the fire out with the wine in my hand.

The black patch near the top is the burn. Around it, rich orange, terracotta and burnt umber layers carry the wax drips and wine stains, with a lone figure turned away in the glow (67 × 48 cm).

I once wrote about it: "I will write the story of this painting. It's not here." This is that story: wax first, then fire, then wine.

title: Elucidated
story:
I painted Elucidated in New Delhi in 2017, and it began with me not knowing what to paint. So I played with new colours, looking for a new feel and a cooler vibe.

It's a square 61 × 61 cm portrait in deep sapphire and cerulean, with green-lit eyes and soft pink lips emerging from near-black shadow.

It came out dark, but it was a really good time for me. After finishing it, I decided to take a break from painting for a while, and about seven or eight months later I moved to Australia.

title: The Conflict of Love and Chastity
medium: Oil & Mixed Media Glaze on Canvas
story:
This was my first painting in Australia, and the next one after Elucidated. When I got there, I didn't paint at all for a few months. Then, around the end of my first semester, I bought canvases and paints and started this one. It took me almost two years to finish.

Everything was changing for me then: the country I lived in, the culture around me and my personal life. In this painting I took classical Renaissance portraiture and looked at it through a modern, digital-age lens. I showed it in the 2020 Love exhibition at White Rhino Artspace in Sydney.

On a 61 × 61 cm square canvas, luminous yellow-ochre highlights and flushed pinks sit against deep cerulean and indigo shadows. The strongest moment is a sharp, deliberate colour "glitch" sliced across the bridge of the nose and the face, breaking the classical symmetry.

That glitch is the tug-of-war inside us between raw, impulsive passion (Love) and the discipline we impose on ourselves (Chastity). It shows how who we are cracks and resets under emotional pressure.

title: Study of Balance
story:
I made Study of Balance in Sydney a few months after The Conflict of Love and Chastity, in the solitude and intensity of life abroad. It was a big change of direction for me, into fluid paint and resin. It sold to a private collector in Melbourne in 2020, but it meant so much to my journey that I bought it back in 2023.

Across a sweeping 51 × 122 cm panorama, deep indigo, ocean blue and luminous currents flow over clean white space, frozen in place under an ultra-clear, glass-like coat of resin. Working with resin meant giving up the control of a brush and dealing with thickness, gravity and curing in real time.

For me it's about control and letting go. It mirrors my own search for grounding and balance in a turbulent, unfamiliar place: learning when to guide the current and when to let the material find its own level.

title: Querencia
medium: Mixed Media (Oil/Acrylic) & Acrylic Gold Paint on Stretched Canvas
story:
I finished Querencia in Sydney in May 2021. It's where the idea of an inner sanctuary, which I first explored in Sneak Peak back in 2014, finally came together. The name comes from the Spanish word querencia: the exact spot in the bullring where the bull feels completely safe and grounded, and gathers its deepest strength. For me it closed a decade of looking inward.

An expressive, graphic figurative portrait sits on a radiant background that I painted in acrylic gold. The intimate black-and-white line work meets the gold, and its sheen changes with the light in the room.

Querencia is a mind that has finally found its home within itself. Once I had that peace and that inner sanctuary, I was ready to turn my eyes outward, towards the systems and absurdities of the global marketplace.

title: Richie Make Money
medium: Mixed Media (Oil, Acrylic & Street Pop) on Canvas
story:
I painted Richie Make Money back in my home studio in Pilani after years in Sydney, and it's where I stepped out of my own head and into the market. I had healed the agony of my youth and found my sanctuary in Querencia, so I moved from looking at the pain of existing to questioning the rules we live by.

It explodes with high-voltage Pop Art colour: vivid orange, kelly green, canary yellow, cobalt blue and crisp white. On the large 121 × 91 cm canvas, the cartoon billionaire Richie Rich stands clutching a sack overflowing with Indian rupee (₹) notes, in front of a Monopoly-style marquee that boldly reads "MAKE MONEY".

There's a sharp irony between my first painting in 2011, Complex Agony, and this return in 2022: both are about desire and survival, but seen from opposite ends of the telescope. With nostalgia and street-pop satire, this one questions late-stage capitalism's endless chase for money and asks how modern society reduces a person's dignity and worth to a bank balance.

title: Richie Carrying Gifts & High Fashion Brands
medium: Mixed Media & Authentic Luxury Brand Packaging Collage on Canvas
story:
I made Richie Carrying Gifts & High Fashion Brands in my 2024–2025 studio cycle, pushing the Richie story into a maximalist 3D critique of hyper-consumerism, brand worship and modern "flex culture".

On a commanding 120 × 90 cm vertical canvas, I collaged real luxury shopping bags and packaging boxes, cut apart, straight onto the surface, alongside graffiti-style lettering. Surrounded by the logos of Hermès, Rolex, Patek Philippe, Richard Mille and Miu Miu, Richie Rich strains under a towering stack of designer gift boxes.

By showing the ultimate symbol of wealth literally weighed down by status symbols, I'm asking a question for our times: are high-fashion logos real armour for our insecurities, or just expensive baggage? It completes my fifteen-year journey, from the teenager rubbing oil paint into raw canvas in a school art room to someone taking apart the theatre of global luxury.
